verified.title: PR-to-issue and ticket-to-ticket links are matched only by key string, in a corpus where the same key belongs to many unrelated documents, so the issue documents themselves contradict the expected link
verified.evidence: units() builds `lin` keyed by the key string (l.189). A PR becomes a unit when exactly one of its linked_linear keys has a document in the pool (l.202-203); tickets work the same way (l.207-209). Keys are reused heavily in the benchmark: 5,060 of 22,703 Linear keys have more than one document (ENG-4821 has 52, ENG-314159 has 108). Requiring exactly one matching key in a 5k or 20k sample favours exactly these reused keys. Read-only check over all five sets: in 40 of the 50 pr_issue/issue_pr_author questions (38 of the 44 held out), the target Linear document lists its own PRs and the question's PR is not among them. Examples: mdtest ENG-4821 ('Guardrails: cooldown windows...') names pr-23777/23795/23944/24012/928, yet all 8 mdtest pr_issue questions reach it from PRs 221089, 28522, 913, 149331, 82145, 18458, 18478 and 35489, whose titles are unrelated. In mdwords issue_pr_author-author-017, ENG-4828 lists related_prs pr-566-add-upgrade-diagnostics-bundle, which exists in the corpus with author Ethan Park and links ENG-4828; the expected answer is 'Aisha Bello' from PR #488 ('Add dashboard panels for hardware profile...'). In 34 of 35 pr_issue questions the PR lists 2-3 Linear keys while the question assumes one ('the Linear issue that PR #n is linked to'). ticket_link: in 38 of 42 questions the target key has several documents in the corpus, and only 1 of 42 targets mentions its source. The source text sometimes contradicts the target: mdtest ENG-4829 and ENG-4833 call ENG-4827 'exporter normalization' and 'routing enforcement', but the ENG-4827 in the set is 'Reconcile Stripe/NetSuite exports and fix proration'; mdtrain ENG-64829 'reuse parts of ENG-4721's load tooling' points at the set's ENG-4721 'misc-chores-office-inventory-and-keycard-cleanup'. The BLIND wording 'Ticket {k} is linked to one other ticket' (l.159) is false for all 3 mdblind uses: ENG-21648 and PM-70012 each link 3 tickets, SUP-901337 links 2.
verified.impact: The link group (17-21 questions per set, about 40% of every published mean) mostly rewards joining unrelated documents on a shared key string. Every arm is graded against the same answers, so the published arm-versus-arm differences and rule outcomes are computed consistently. But claims such as 'learned plans follow links between documents' have little support. If answers were checked against the documents' own links, roughly 38 of 44 held-out PR↔issue questions and about 38 of 42 ticket questions would have no valid in-set answer. Link-group scores (for example retest v4 link 0.524, blind v4 0.556) would then fall to near what the few genuine pairs allow.

verdict.reason:
I checked the reviewer's facts and most of them are accurate. Link keys are reused across the corpus: 52 Linear files in EnterpriseRAG-Bench/generated_data/sources/linear have key ENG-4821, and 30 have ENG-4827. All 8 mdtest pr_issue questions resolve to the same ENG-4821 document. Its 'Related PRs' list names PRs 23777, 24012, 23944, 23795 and 928, and none of those is the question's PR. In mdwords, ENG-4828 mentions pr-566. The three BLIND questions that say 'Ticket {k} is linked to one other ticket' have 3, 2 and 3 keys in the source ticket's link fields.

The facts are right, but the defect claimed from them does not follow. Each arm's fact bank is built only from that set's 49 or 50 documents (factbank_build.json 'sources' is 49 or 50). questions() rebuilds `lin` and `tick` from those documents only.

What I checked inside the sets, read-only:
(1) No set has two documents with the same key. Across mdtrain, mdtest, mdfresh, mdwords and mdblind there are 0 duplicate (source, key) pairs. So the key join in each set is unambiguous.
(2) No question's PR mentions any other in-set key, anywhere in its record.
(3) No issue_pr_author target mentions any in-set PR other than the expected one. ENG-4828's pr-566 is not in mdwords, and it is the only PR there that references ENG-4828 is #488. Several targets do mention other PRs, but all of those are outside the set.
(4) Of 42 ticket_link sources, 39 list several link keys, and every time exactly one of them is in the set.

So each question has exactly one answer that can be reached from the documents given. That answer comes from following an explicit link field (linked_linear, linked_issues, dependencies, and so on) to the only document with that key, and it is the expected answer. The 'contradictions' are with documents that are not in the haystack, which no arm sees.

A partial 'Related PRs' list, or a different description of a key in free text, does not cancel the PR's own explicit link. The pre-registrations also define link questions this way ('a pull request → its Linear issue', 'every expected answer is computed within its own set').

The reviewer's corrected impact rests on a different rule that was never pre-registered: answers would have to agree with the target's own back-links or topic. Under that rule, questions would have to be dropped. It is not evidence that the current scores are wrong. The planner hops on key references and is graded on whether it reaches the right in-set document. That is what 'follows links' means here, and it is measured correctly.

The BLIND wording problem is a slightly inaccurate phrase written by an independent writer. It does not change any expected answer.

The underlying cause, key collisions, is a property of the external synthetic corpus, not a bug in units() or questions().
verdict.corrected_impact:
The published expected answers and arm comparisons stand. Within each 50-document set the link answers are unique and correct.

There is a separate, smaller problem: the reused hub keys concentrate questions on a few documents. In units(), `lin[ks[0]]` points every PR that names ENG-4821 at the same document. The pr_issue targets per set:
- mdtest: all 8 are ENG-4821, so there are only 3 distinct expected answers.
- mdfresh: 4 of 8 are ENG-8421.
- mdblind: 4 of 8 are ENG-4821.
- mdtrain: 6 of 11 ticket_link targets are ENG-314159.

This means pr_issue in each set is effectively fewer independent items than the question count suggests. Per-kind link scores are therefore noisier, with all-or-nothing swings when one document is read right or wrong. This adds noise but does not favour any arm, and no pre-registered rule outcome changes because of it.

verified.title: Units are capped per kind but not per target document, so one hub issue answers most of a set's link questions (and the held-out set got no issue_pr_author questions)
verified.evidence: split() (l.231) and fresh() (l.325) allow at most 8 units of each kind but place no limit on how many units share the same target document. split() keeps units that share a document in the same set. Reproduced split() exactly from hay5k_docs.json: the haystack has 14 PR units with only 5 distinct issues, 9 of them pointing at the same ENG-4821 document (dsid ...f2aacb). All 8 mdtest pr_issue questions go through that one document, plus ticket_link-status-036: 9 of 17 link questions, whose expected values repeat ('Done' x3, '2025-04-15' x3, 'Keiko Yamamoto' x2). Because 8 PRs reference ENG-4821, the refs==1 test (l.273-274) removes every issue_pr_author question, so mdtest has 0 (the pre-registration's 'none held out' limit). The other sets: mdtrain ticket_link 6 of 11 target one ENG-314159 document; mdfresh link has 21 questions but 10 distinct targets (ENG-8421 x5, ENG-4821 x4); mdblind ENG-4821 x5 of 18. Action questions: mdtest has 9 with only 2 distinct expected answers (6 identical, all Maya Chen's issues); mdtrain has 8 with 4 (5 identical). The repeated questions really do move together: in mdblind, pr_issue-status-018 and -040 both target ENG-4821, and both v4 and v6 flip together from 0 to 1 between the held-out and changed copies.
verified.impact: The effective sample sizes are much smaller than the published counts. In mdtest one document carries 9/17 of the link group: a single document-level success or failure moves link by up to 0.53 and the mean by about 0.18. That is larger than the 0.05-0.20 thresholds of every pre-registered rule, so per-kind and per-group differences (for example mdtest v2 pr_issue 0.375 = 3 questions on the same document) say little about generalisation. None of the published rule outcomes was shown to flip from this alone, but the margins are within what one hub document can swing.

verdict.reason: The counts hold up; parts of the impact claim do not. Code: split() (factbank_multi.py l.219-236) and fresh() (l.317-329) limit only kinds_in[kind] >= 8. Nothing limits how many units share a target document. I re-ran units()/split() on scratchpad/hay5k_docs.json and got exactly the frozen mdtrain/mdtest dsids. There are 14 pr units but only 5 distinct issues, and 9 of them point at ENG-4821 (dsid_d7aeb7de...f2aacb); 8 of those went to the test set. mdtest: dsid f2aacb is in the gold docs of 9 of the 17 link questions (all 8 pr_issue plus ticket_link-status-036). Because 8 PRs in the set reference ENG-4821, the refs==1 test (l.273-274) leaves no issue_pr_author question. Other sets: mdtrain has 6 of 11 ticket_link questions on one ENG-314159 doc (dsid a56bbe...); mdfresh's top documents are in 5 and 4 of its 21 link questions; mdblind has dsid cb07d684 (ENG-4821) in 5 of 18. Action questions: mdtest has 9 with 2 distinct expected answers (6 identical); mdtrain has 8 with 4 (5 identical). This clustering is not disclosed. The results doc only says 'one question moves a kind's score by 0.11-0.25', which assumes the questions are independent. What does not hold or is not new: (1) The 0 issue_pr_author held-out questions are already listed in FACTBANK_MULTI_PREREGISTRATION.md Known limits ('none held out'); the hub is only the cause. (2) The 'move together' example is the already-known rename defect. In mdblindchanged the expected 'In Progress' became 'Cosima Abernathy' for pr_issue-status-018 and -040 (and ticket_link-status-035). v4 and v6 answer that same name, so they flip from 0 to 1. (3) Questions on one hub document do not succeed or fail as a block. In mdtest, v2 got the 3 status questions right and all 5 due_date/assignee questions wrong; v3 got 0 of 9. The correlated unit is (document, field), so the 'one document swings link by 0.53' figure is an upper bound that no arm reached.
verdict.corrected_impact:
No published number is wrong: every figure is the pre-registered per-question mean on the frozen sets. No published decision flips either. I rescored with hub questions de-duplicated: link questions grouped by target key, PR-author questions by PR, action questions by expected answer, and each group's average counted once. The results were:
- First test: rule 1 +0.064 (published +0.070), rule 2 -0.243 (-0.226), rule 3 0.000. Same outcomes.
- Retest: rule 1 +0.51, rule 2 +0.38, rule 3 -0.28, rule 4 0.000. Same outcomes.
- New-words test: rule 1 -0.042, rule 2 -0.33, rule 3 met, rule 4 met. Same outcomes.

What the hub does change is how some published per-kind statements should be read:
- The first test's v2 held-out link score of 0.176 is exactly the 3 pr_issue status questions on the one ENG-4821 document.
- In the retest, 4 of the 5 v4 misses for 'pull request -> Linear issue' (0.375) are on one ENG-8421 document: 3 due_date questions and 1 assignee question. The published reading 'ranked the due date below other fields' is therefore one document counted three times.

The general-English test (mdblind/general_report, not yet written up in docs) is the one place where it matters. Its rule 3 is published as not met at -0.158 against -0.15. With the hub questions de-duplicated it becomes -0.128, which would be met. But that margin (0.008) is smaller than one question's weight (about 0.014-0.019 on the mean), so the rule is borderline whether or not the hub is counted.

The fair caveat: the true number of independent link items is smaller than the published counts (for example, about 9 distinct targets for mdtest's 17 link questions). The 0.53/0.18 swing is an upper bound, not something that was observed.

verified.title: Action-item owners are joined to Linear assignees by name string, so customer attendees inherit a same-named Redwood engineer's issues
verified.evidence: units() (l.212-215) and questions() (l.291-296) take the owner string from the meeting action item and look it up in by_person, which is keyed by the Linear assignee name, with nothing else to tell people apart. Checked against each meeting's attendee lists: in 14 of 43 action_owner_issues questions the owner is a customer attendee. That is mdtrain 5/8 (017, 021, 023, 024, 028), mdfresh 3/9 (021, 023, 037), mdwords 3/8 (034, 035, 036) and mdblind 3/9 (024, 028, 031); mdblind 042 lists Ravi Shah on both sides. Yet each expected answer is the internal Linear issues of a same-named assignee. mdtrain maps five different 'Priya Nair's to the same DES-9512, ENG-11097, ENG-88763: Platform Eng at Orion Research, Security Lead at Hearthwell Diagnostics, Head of ML at Aperture Analytics, Redwood SRE and Redwood Solutions Engineer.
verified.impact: These questions reward joining on the name string where a person reading the documents would say the owner has no Linear issues. v4 gets credit on 4 of the 5 in training (about 0.17 of the training combine group, about 0.06 of the mean), 2 of 3 in the retest (about 0.03 of the mean), 1 of 3 in the new-words set and 2 of 3 in the blind set (about 0.03 of the mean). No pre-registered rule outcome flips; the plan weights for this kind were learned largely from these conflated examples.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. The code does what the reviewer says. units() (factbank_multi.py l.211-215) and questions() (l.290-296) take the owner string from memory_test.action_items(). action_items() strips any trailing parenthetical such as "(Orion)" or "(Theta)", and the result is looked up in by_person, which is keyed only by the Linear assignee name. Nothing checks redwood_attendees or customer_attendees.

I read each meeting in the data. Of the 43 action_owner_issues questions (mdtrain 8, mdtest 9, mdfresh 9, mdwords 8, mdblind 9), the owner is listed among customer_attendees in exactly 14:
- mdtrain: 017, 021, 023, 024, 028
- mdfresh: 021, 023, 037
- mdwords: 034, 035, 036
- mdblind: 024, 028, 031
- mdtest: none

mdblind 042 does list Ravi Shah on both sides. The action items themselves are customer tasks, and some say so outright: "Priya Nair (Orion) - provide anonymized logs and hot prefixes", "Priya Sharma (Theta): Provide list of required compliance artifacts", "Marco Reyes: Provide Constellation's data residency spec". In mdtrain, 017, 021 and 023 are customer people at three different companies (Orion Research, Hearthwell Diagnostics, Aperture Analytics) with three different titles. 034 is a Redwood SRE and 035 a Redwood Solutions Engineer. All five map to the same DES-9512, ENG-11097 and ENG-88763, so they cannot all be the true owner. The Linear teams are Redwood's own (engineering, design, product-management).

One argument against: the benchmark has no real person identity. Only 186 of 2,996 sampled Linear assignees are in employee_directory.yaml, and none of the 14 owner names are there. Even so, giving a customer attendee's action item the Redwood Linear tickets of someone with the same name is a wrong expected answer by any reading of the documents. The reviewer's credit counts are right. v4 is scored 1.0 on mdtrain 017, 021, 023 and 028 and 0 on 024. On mdfresh it gets 021 and 037. On mdwords it gets 036. On mdblind it gets 024 and 028.

One part of the claimed impact is overstated. Whether a rule flips depends on how these questions are handled:
- If they are dropped, no pre-registered rule changes outcome.
- If they are scored as wrong (the owner really has no Linear issues), one rule does flip: general-test rule 3 (v6 test >= v6 training - 0.15). It fails now at 0.769 vs 0.927, a gap of -0.158, and would pass at 0.741 vs 0.869, a gap of -0.128. That outcome sits only in mdblind/general_report.json; docs/FACTBANK_GENERAL_RESULTS.md does not exist yet.
verdict.corrected_impact:
The published means in docs/FACTBANK_MULTI_RESULTS.md and docs/FACTBANK_WORDS_RESULTS.md all include the 14 conflated questions: training v4/v5 0.927, retest v4 0.596 and v5 0.631, new-words v4 0.611 and v5 0.576. How much they move depends on how the questions are treated.

**Dropped (the likeliest fix, since the frozen sets cannot be regenerated):**

| set | arm | published | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| training | v4–v6 | 0.927 | 0.941 |
| retest | v4 | 0.596 | 0.588 |
| retest | v5 | 0.631 | 0.628 |
| retest | v6 | 0.657 | 0.652 |
| new-words | v4 | 0.611 | 0.629 |
| new-words | v5 | 0.576 | 0.594 |
| blind | v4 | 0.727 | 0.737 |
| blind | v6 | 0.769 | 0.778 |

Every pre-registered rule keeps its outcome (multi/retest rules 1-4, words rules 1-4, general rules 1-5).

**Scored as wrong (the owner has no Linear issues):**
- Training v4/v5/v6 drop by 0.058, the retest by 0.032, new-words by 0.014 and blind by 0.028.
- Published rules still keep their outcomes, with wide margins.
- The one exception is general-test rule 3 ("principles, not memorisation"), which goes from not met (-0.158) to met (-0.128). It currently misses by only 0.008 and is not yet written up in a results doc.

The first held-out test (mdtest) has no conflated questions, and v3 scores 0 on every action question, so the first test's rules are unaffected. Five of the 8 training action questions are conflated, but the plan they teach (meeting → owner → assignee → issues) is the same one the 3 clean examples teach. So any effect on the learned weights is likely small.

verified.title: Fresh-name pool makes far more people share a first or last name than in the original, which flipped one answer
verified.evidence: Lines 53-57 and 175-179 give every person a name from 28 first names x 20 last names. Each set has 103-113 people, so the changed copies have many more pairs of people sharing a first name or last name. Counted from renamed.json, excluding status and 'Role:' entries. First-name pairs, original -> changed: mdchanged 79->185, mdfreshchanged 89->203, mdwordschanged 102->217, mdblindchanged 69->192. Last-name pairs: 103->247, 75->278, 163->300, 128->246. Of the person_count/person_first questions in each set, 9-11 (out of 12-16) get a new name that shares a word with more people than the original did. Example: Jonah Kim shares a word with 1 person; his new name Saoirse Varga shares one with 11. A concrete flip: mdtest person_first-016 asks about Rafael Ortega. v2 answers PM-50724, which is correct. In mdchanged he becomes 'Odalys Ashdown', and Ben Cho (assignee of PM-25671) becomes 'Odalys Iqbal'. The original names share no word. On the changed copy v2 puts the 'Odalys Iqbal' sentence of PM-25671 first and answers PM-25671, scoring 0. The bank's evidence shows '[person] Odalys Ashdown' found correctly, ranked below that sentence.
verified.impact: It is the only score difference between held-out and changed in mdtest besides the known issues. v2 on the changed copy fell from combine 0.080 to 0.040 and mean 0.085 to 0.072 (mdtest/multi_report.json). No pre-registered rule uses v2. v3-v6 scores are identical across all four pairs, apart from the known 'In Progress' flips in mdblind. The extra name ambiguity makes the changed copy harder, so 'holds when the information changes' is biased toward failing, not passing. It also means the changed copy is not equivalent to the original for any method that matches names word by word.

verdict.reason:
I couldn't refute this one. Every part of the evidence checks out.

1. The code: the pool is still `fresh = [f"{a} {b}" for a in FIRST for b in LAST]`, 28 first names × 20 last names. That is line 175 before commit 9897d23 and line 189 now (cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_split.py). The in-progress fix (commit 9897d23, which made the `_fixed` copies) does not touch the pool.

2. Pair counts from each copy's renamed.json. With the five 'Role:' entries removed and statuses left in, I get first-name pairs 80→191 for mdchanged and last-name pairs 103→259, close to the reviewer's figures. The fixed copies, which contain no statuses, show the same inflation:
   - first-name pairs: 88→201, 103→225, 104→225, 69→190
   - last-name pairs: 111→259, 83→309, 163→309, 128→244

   That is about what a pool this small gives at random: for about 105 people, C(105,2)/28 ≈ 195 first-name pairs and /20 ≈ 273 last-name pairs.

3. Person questions: of the person_count/person_first questions, the new name shares a word with more people than the old name did in 10/16, 10/12, 11/15 and 9/15 (the fixed copies give 12/16, 8/12, 11/15 and 9/15).

4. The flip is real and caused by the shared word. Scoring every version across all eight held-out/changed pairs with factbank_test.direct, the only differences are:
   - v2 on mdtest person_first-016 (1→0), in both mdchanged and mdchanged_fixed. In the fixed copy, Rafael Ortega and Ben Cho again share a first name: Mireille Castellanos and Mireille Lindqvist.
   - the known 'In Progress' flips in mdblind.
   - v1 on mdwords person_first-011 (0→1), fixed copy only (see the corrected impact).

   I reran TrainedBank with fb50/lessons.json on an in-memory copy of mdchanged/factbank_v2.sqlite, opened read-only:
   - It reproduces PM-25671.
   - Renaming only 'Odalys Iqbal' to a name that shares no word gives PM-50724 again, which is correct. Ben Cho's document then drops from first to second in the BM25 seeds.

   So the shared first name 'Odalys' causes the error.

Caveats that weaken the reviewer's wording (they don't refute the defect):
- In the original, Rafael Ortega already shared a word with three people (Rafael Mendes, Rafael Ortiz, Miguel Ortega).
- The reverse test, renaming Ben Cho to 'Rafael Cho' in the original, does not flip the answer. So a shared word is not enough by itself; the effect depends on BM25 word weights.
verdict.corrected_impact:
No pre-registered decision changes:
- The multi-document 'holds when the information changes' rules use v3, v4, v5 and v6. Those scores are identical between held-out and changed in all four pairs, apart from the known 'In Progress' flips in mdblind.
- The learning test's rule 2 uses v2 and the same name pool. It was met at −0.017 against a threshold of −0.05 (FACTBANK_LEARNING_RESULTS.md), so any extra difficulty only narrowed the margin.

One published non-rule number is affected. The committed docs/benchmarks/factbank_multi/multi_report.md/.json shows v2 on the changed copy at:
- combine 0.040, against 0.080 held-out
- mean 0.072, against 0.085
- person_first 0.125, against 0.25

That whole difference comes from person_first-016, and the in-memory test shows the shared 'Odalys' causes it. The headline table in FACTBANK_MULTI_RESULTS.md does not report v2 on the changed copy.

The claim that the changed copy is 'biased toward failing' goes too far. Name changes from this pool move scores both ways: in mdwordschanged_fixed, v1 on person_first-011 went from 0 to 1. I did not test whether a shared word caused that one. The accurate statement is this: the changed copies have about 2 to 3.7 times as many people sharing a first or last name as the originals. That makes them non-equivalent for name-word matching, and it can move individual answers. It produced one downward flip, and so far it has not changed any rule outcome.

verified.title: Single-key answers (compare_two, person_first) get F1 partial credit instead of exact-match scoring, so listing several keys earns 0.4-0.667
verified.evidence: direct() returns c['f1'] whenever check() (cie/src/cie/eval/memory_test.py:1045-1050) took the 'ids' path. compare_two and person_first expect exactly one key ({'ids':[first],'id_kind':'key'}, factbank_multi.py:289 and :303), so they are scored by F1 like the list kind. Reproduction: direct({'expected':{'ids':['ENG-12109'],'id_kind':'key'}}, 'PM-99977, ENG-12109') = 0.667, while plans.matches() on the same input = False (training labels use exact match, so training and test disagree on what is right). Giving all 4 keys for a person_first question scores 0.4. In the data: mdchanged_fixed v4 gives 4 person_first answers with two keys each, scored 0.667 each: person_first-004 'DES-12901, ENG-4827' for ['DES-12901'], plus -006, -012 and -016. Across all 13 work folders, no other partial score appears on a single-key question. The pre-registrations say 'values and dates must match exactly; lists score F1', and FACTBANK_MULTI_RESULTS labels only the action-item kind as F1.
verified.impact: No pre-registered decision or published report number changes: every partial case is in a set that has not been published. The fixed first-test copy's v4 score in scratch general/changed_fixed_check.json (all_fixed v4 = 0.675) would be 0.640 with exact scoring (combine 0.747 -> 0.640), which widens the gap to v5/v6 (0.693) from 0.018 to 0.053. The flaw can matter later: answering 'A, B' to every compare question scores 0.667 each, which beats the expected 0.5 from guessing one key. Across the group that adds up to +0.222 on the mean, and it rewards exactly the copy-from-the-question failure diagnosed for v3. The general test's rule 3 misses by only 0.008, so a scoring artefact this size could flip a decision.

verdict.reason: I could not refute it, and every part checked out. (1) Code: direct() (cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_test.py:159-161) returns c['f1'] whenever check() has computed one. check() (memory_test.py:1045-1050) computes F1 for any expected 'ids', with no exception for one key. compare_two (factbank_multi.py:303) and person_first (:289) both expect one key, {'ids':[first],'id_kind':'key'}. (2) Reproduction: direct({'ids':['ENG-12109']}, 'PM-99977, ENG-12109') = 0.667, while plans.matches() on the same input is False. Answering with 4 real-looking keys, one of them right, scores 0.4. One caution: matches() also uses exact match for the multi-key action-item lists, so the train/test mismatch is not limited to single-key questions. (3) Data: I scanned all 13 md* work folders and every factbank*.jsonl version. On single-key questions, partial scores occur only in mdchanged_fixed factbank_v4: person_first-004 'DES-12901, ENG-4827', -006 'PM-56217, PM-903456', -012 'DES-350721, ENG-213999' and -016 'ENG-13579, PM-50724', each 0.667. (4) Recompute: I scored mdchanged_fixed in memory with exact match for single-key questions, without writing any file. v4 combine goes from 0.747 to 0.640 and the v4 mean from 0.675 to 0.640; person_first by kind goes from 0.584 to 0.25. (5) Documents: the multi pre-registration calls the measure 'the memory test's code check', which is what the code does. That check was written for the memory test, where list answers had 2 to 10 items, so single-key questions did not exist there. All four fact-bank pre-registrations say 'values and dates must match exactly; lists score F1', and FACTBANK_MULTI_RESULTS marks only the action-item kind as '(F1)' in a column headed 'right'. Scoring a one-key answer by F1 therefore goes beyond what was pre-registered, and it gives credit for hedged answers.
verdict.corrected_impact: No published number or pre-registered decision changes. Every partial score on a single-key question is in mdchanged_fixed v4, which no document in docs/ cites. The first test's changed-copy rule uses v3 (0.083, unaffected), so the v4 figure is not an input to any rule. In scratch general/changed_fixed_check.json, the first test's all_fixed v4 would fall from 0.675 to 0.640 (combine 0.747 to 0.640). That widens the gap to v5/v6 (0.693) from 0.018 to 0.053. The published reports (mdtest multi_report, mdfresh retest_report, mdwords words_report, mdblind general_report) have no partial scores on single-key questions, so their numbers are the same under exact scoring. The risk is for later runs: answering both keys from a compare question scores 0.667 there, and 0 under exact scoring. Over the whole compare group that adds +0.222 to the three-group mean compared with no answer, and +0.056 compared with guessing one key at random (expected 0.5). That is enough to flip a rule decided by a small margin.

verified.title: The company lexicon used by v5 and v6 in the general-English test contains 24 of that test's 50 documents
verified.evidence: lexicon.build() leaves out only the dsids of the --exclude folders. lexicon200k_w2.npz was built on 2026-10-07 at 18:31 with mt5k + mdfresh + mdwords excluded (5,189 documents; the file's info says excluded_documents 5189). The general-English set (mdblind, seed 29) was drawn on 2026-10-08 at 00:46. factbank_multi.build_fresh (lines 354-355) excluded only the same 5,189 documents and never the lexicon's 200k sample. Reproduction: lexicon.sample(mt5k/index.json, those 5,189 dsids, 200000, 23) rebuilds the lexicon's sample exactly. Its sentence count comes out at 11,547,042, which matches info['sentences']. That sample holds 24 of the 50 mdblind dsids (15 linear, 6 github, 2 fireflies, 1 jira), which give 1,370 sentences. 35 of the 50 blind questions have a gold document among them. build()'s people and status loop (lines 395-404) also read every non-excluded ticket, so it read the test tickets too. docs/FACTBANK_GENERAL_PREREGISTRATION.md says no document of any test set is used. v4 is unaffected because it uses no lexicon. The retest and new-words sets do not overlap the sample (0 of 50 each). Process note: early in this audit I created a folder scratchpad/audit_leak holding four probe scripts, then deleted it. Every later check ran from stdin. git status is clean and no other file was created, changed or deleted.
verified.impact: The pre-registered statement is false, but I measured no effect on any number. I rebuilt the lexicon in memory, without writing a file: same sample minus the 24 test documents (11,545,672 sentences), window 2, float16 round trip. v5 and v6 then gave exactly the published answers on mdblind and mdblindchanged: 0 of 50 differ each time, and the means stay 0.769, 0.769, 0.769 and 0.806. No rule of the general-English test changes. The documentation needs correcting, and later sets should leave out the lexicon's sample.

verdict.reason:
The leak is real: I confirmed it from the code and the data. lexicon.build() (cie/src/cie/factbank/lexicon.py:380) leaves out only the dsids of the --exclude folders. factbank_multi.build_fresh (cie/src/cie/eval/factbank_multi.py:354-355) leaves out only the same 5,189 haystack documents (mt5k 5,089, mdfresh 50, mdwords 50) and never the lexicon's 200k sample. The lexicon file is dated 2026-10-07 18:31 and mdblind/haystack.json 2026-10-08 00:46, so the test set was drawn after the lexicon was frozen.

Reproduction: L.sample(mt5k/index.json, those 5,189 dsids, 200000, 23) gives 200,001 dsids. Running texts_of over them gives exactly 11,547,042 sentences, which equals info['sentences'] in lexicon200k_w2.npz. The sample holds 24 of the 50 mdblind dsids (linear 15, github 6, fireflies 2, jira 1), which give 1,370 sentences. 35 of the 50 blind questions have a gold document among those 24. mdfresh, mdwords, mdtest, mdtrain and mt5k each overlap 0.

Independent proof that the published file really contains those sentences: I ran typing() over the sample without the blind documents and over the 1,370 blind sentences, with the same people and status sets. The two counts add up exactly to the published info['typed'] {num 8428536, who 3880169, when 1877650, state 77697}.

The people and status loop (lines 395-404) also reads every non-excluded ticket, so it read 42 of the 50 blind documents. Leaving them out changes nothing, though: still 60,210 people and the same 16 statuses.

So the company lexicon used by v5 and v6 in the general-English test was built partly from that test's documents. That contradicts FACTBANK_WORDS_PREREGISTRATION.md, which says the lexicon may use "no document of any test set", and the general preregistration's "no document of any test set", which reuses v5 "exactly as tested". The general preregistration's line sits under the general-English counts section, so it can be read narrowly. The violation of the project's stated rule for the lexicon stands either way. The claims and numbers are confirmed; it is a documentation and procedure defect, not a scoring defect.
verdict.corrected_impact:
No published number or decision changes. I first checked the setup: the published lexicon with the published plan lessons reproduces every published v5 and v6 answer (0 differ on mdtrain, mdfresh, mdwords, mdblind, mdblindchanged and mdblindchanged_fixed), and retraining reproduces the published weights exactly.

I then rebuilt the lexicon in memory without writing any file. I removed the 24 blind documents from the sample (11,545,672 sentences) and all 50 from the people and status loop, used window 2, and did a float16 and JSON round trip. The vocabulary differs by 4 words of 40,000. Among the 39 known words, similarities move by at most 0.0013.

Both with the frozen plan lessons and after retraining on mdtrain (the weights come out identical, max difference 0.0), v5 and v6 give 0 differing answers on every set above. So the general-English test's means stay as published: test set v5 0.769 and v6 0.769; changed copy v5 0.769 and v6 0.806 (0.769 with the fixed copy); retest v6 0.657. All five rule outcomes are unchanged.

What should change: the preregistration and the lexicon description should say that 24 of the general-English test's 50 documents (1,370 of 11.5M sentences) were in the company lexicon's sample. Later test sets should also leave out the lexicon's sample, not just the earlier haystacks. The reviewer's figures (24 of 50, 15/6/2/1 by source, 1,370 sentences, 35 of 50 questions, 0 of 50 answers differ) all check out.

unverified.title: ticket_link answers are ambiguous when another in-set ticket links back or the source text references a different in-set ticket
unverified.evidence: Only the source's own outgoing link fields are counted (l.206-209), but the wordings use symmetric verbs ('tied to', 'connected to', 'references'). mdtest ticket_link-status-023 'ENG-4833 is tied to another ticket. Where does that one stand?' expects In Progress (ENG-4827), while ENG-4881, also in the set, lists ENG-4833 in its dependencies and is Done. mdwords ticket_link-status-024 'Which stage is the ticket referenced from ENG-4822 at?' expects In Progress (ENG-4821), but ENG-4822's comment says 'remaining UX polish is tracked in ENG-4828' (in set, In Review), and ENG-4823 (Done) depends on ENG-4822. mdtest ticket_link-assignee-021: ENG-4829's text also mentions the set's ENG-4821.
unverified.impact: About 3 questions have a second defensible answer. In the published runs no arm gave the alternative answer, so no published number changes. A better arm could be marked wrong on them, at about 1/17-1/19 of a link group.

unverified.title: Duplicate keys inside a set are silently collapsed, so expected answers and person counts would ignore one of the documents
unverified.evidence: questions() (l.248) and units() (l.189-190) key `lin`/`tick` by key string, so the last document with a key wins. Neither split() nor fresh() rejects a set that holds two documents with the same key, although the corpus has 5,060 duplicated Linear keys and the 5k haystack has 12 (ENG-4821 x2, ENG-4829 x4, PM-9814 x2...). Synthetic reproduction: two documents 'ENG-100' (Ann Lee, Bob Ray), a third 'ENG-200' (Ann Lee) and a PR linking ENG-100. The PR question expects 'Bob Ray' with gold ['b','p'], although Ann Lee's ENG-100 is in the set. Ann Lee's two issues are counted as one, so she gets no person questions.
unverified.impact: None for the published sets: all five held-out/training sets have 0 duplicate keys and 0 duplicate PR numbers. It would give ambiguous or wrong expected answers in any future fresh() draw that happens to include two same-key documents.

unverified.title: ISO timestamps (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm) are never date-shifted; every meeting keeps its original recorded_at
unverified.evidence: _ISO = r"\b(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})\b" needs a word boundary after the day. In '2026-07-13T15:00:00Z' the 'T' follows a digit, so there is no boundary and nothing matches. Repro: shift_dates('recorded_at 2026-07-13T15:00:00Z | Date: 2026-07-13 15:00 UTC') returns 'recorded_at 2026-07-13T15:00:00Z | Date: 2026-08-05 15:00 UTC'. I compared every date field the fact bank reads (bank._is_date_field, parsed with parse_when) between original and changed documents. 123-127 per copy are shifted by 23 days. 8 per copy are not: fireflies recorded_at in all 32 meetings, e.g. mdfreshchanged '2026-07-09T14:00:00-07:00' unchanged. 6 more timestamps in text are unshifted: mdtest transcript 1, mdfresh jira logs 1, mdblind jira logs_and_dashboards 2, jira description 1, linear incident_summary 1. The bank stores the unshifted date. In mdchanged/factbank_v2.sqlite the Elysium meeting's sources.date is '2026-07-13', the same as in mdtest. Yet its transcript header now reads 2026-08-05 and its action items are due 23 days later. All four pre-registrations say 'every ISO date moved 23 days later'.
unverified.impact: No published number changes. No question asks a meeting date. Regenerating all 200 changed questions from the changed documents (factbank_multi.questions with the same seeds and wordings) reproduces questions.jsonl exactly. Per-question v1-v6 scores show no flip from this. The changed copies still contradict themselves: a meeting is dated 23 days before its own header and action items. Any later question about meeting dates or 'due N days after the meeting' would get wrong expected answers. The in-progress fix does not touch this.

unverified.title: Only names from top-level people fields are renamed; first-name references and names that appear only in text keep the originals
unverified.evidence: changed() collects people only from top-level PEOPLE_FIELDS values that person_name accepts, plus expected values. rename() then replaces only exact full names and their lower_underscore and lower.dot forms. Counted in the changed documents: 28 (mdchanged), 29, 34 and 42 (mdblindchanged) different full names that look like people stay unrenamed, mostly in free text. Examples: "Liam O'Connor" x4 and 'Naomi Feldman' x2. A stakeholders string has 'Riz Ahmed (infra)' next to renamed colleagues, because person_name rejects the whole 'PM: ...; Eng: ...' string. About 460-600 standalone first names of renamed people also remain per copy. mdchanged has 'Maya' 110 times, 'Diego' 80 and 'Priya' 53, while 'Maya Chen' became 'Dashiell Abernathy'. Transcript line '[00:14] Marcus: Marcus Lee.' becomes '[00:14] Marcus: Ottoline Ashdown.'. In PM-50724, '(Owner: Rafael) - due 2025-09-17' keeps 'Rafael' while Rafael Ortega -> Odalys Ashdown. A case-insensitive search with space/_/./- separators finds 0 leftover full forms of renamed names, so the leak is first names and unlisted people.
unverified.impact: Expected answers are not affected: regenerating the questions on the changed documents matches all 200. I found no score flip caused by this. But the claim that every person is renamed is not true. In the changed copy, first-name mentions (owners, speaker labels, work-log lines) point to nobody, while in the original they point to the person. This only matters for text-based arms (v2 text facts, plain search) on future questions.

unverified.title: Date-shaped strings inside identifiers are shifted, but the document paths keep the original dates
unverified.evidence: The \b regex also matches dates after a hyphen inside identifiers and file names, and _walk applies it to every string. Found in original documents: mdtest 'ff-2026-06-30-citri...' (meeting_id) and '...-audit-2026-03-01.csv'. mdfresh: 'CRM-NS-2025-09-17' and 'CP-2026-09-08-03'. mdblind: 11 cases, including 'CHG-2025-10-06' and 'redwood.ai/INC-2026-02-21-gpu-...'. All of these become different identifiers, which memory_test.KEY_RE would read as IDs, e.g. CHG-2025-10-29. Meanwhile index.json is only symlinked (line 191-192), so the 8 fireflies paths per set keep the original date. Example: meeting_id 'ff-2026-06-30-...' becomes 'ff-2026-07-23-...' while the path stays '.../2026-06-30-...json'. The compact meeting_id 'ff-20260713-elysium-01' is not shifted at all. The fact bank stores that path in sources.path.
unverified.impact: No current number changes: no question asks for these identifiers. The asked keys (ENG-, PM-, DES-, SUP-) have no dates, and question regeneration matches exactly. It adds more internal inconsistency to the changed copy.

unverified.title: 'original' gets the transform twice when a question has no original field
unverified.evidence: In HEAD, q['question'] = fn(q['question']) runs first (line 194, working tree 208). Then q['original'] = fn(q.get('original', q['question'])) (line 195, working tree 209) reads the already-changed question and changes it again. Repro: with names {'Maya Chen': ...}, question 'What did Maya Chen promise in the 2026-07-13 call?' gives question '... 2026-08-05 call?' but original '... 2026-08-28 call?', a 46-day shift. None of the 200 multi-document questions had an 'original' field, so every one went through this path.
unverified.impact: No effect on current data. No changed question contains an ISO date, and renaming twice changes nothing, so original equals question for all 200. Nothing in src reads 'original'. It would silently corrupt 'original' for any dated question in a future set.

unverified.title: Value and count answers are scored by containment, not exact match: a list or a sentence that includes the expected value scores 1.0
unverified.evidence: check() marks a 'value' answer correct if the expected value appears anywhere in the answer as a whole word. Reproduction through factbank_test.direct: expected 'Maya Chen', answer 'Devon Price, Maya Chen' -> 1.0; expected 'In Progress', answer 'Done, In Progress' -> 1.0; expected count '2', answer '2 or 4' -> 1.0, 'PR #2' -> 1.0, 'SUP-2' -> 1.0. plans.matches() (plans.py:446-447) returns False for the same inputs. The planner can produce such answers: v3 'single' joins all of the first entity's values (plans.py:197-198), and a 'list' over person labels joins names (plans.py:183-184). The pre-registrations say values must match exactly and a count must be the right number. Count over the 13 work folders, all arms: 0 value answers scored 1.0 without being equal (after normalisation) to the expected value.
unverified.impact: No published number or decision changes today (0 affected answers). This is a latent leniency: any future arm that returns multi-value answers to value questions would be over-credited, up to 1.0 per question.

unverified.title: Results doc describes the 'pieces' measure as the share of questions that have all pieces, but the code reports the mean share of pieces; several published figures are misstated
unverified.evidence: pieces_in() (factbank_multi.py:447-460) returns the fraction of a question's pieces found. measure() averages these fractions per group. The report rows and rule 4 call this 'all pieces within N chars' (factbank_multi.py:525, 607). FACTBANK_MULTI_RESULTS.md:14-15 says the memory bank's evidence 'holds them [all the pieces] for 0.32' of the questions, but 0.315 is the mean share; only 7/50 = 0.14 held-out questions (group mean 0.125) have all pieces within 24,000 characters. Lines 141-142 say v4 'holds all of a question's pieces within its first 2,000 characters for 0.899 of the questions. The figure is 0.699 for v3 and 0.775 for v1.' Counted on mdfresh, the actual shares of questions with all pieces are 43/50 = 0.86, 25/50 = 0.50 and 25/50 = 0.50.
unverified.impact: No decision changes. Rule 4 is met under either reading: on the all-pieces basis, v3 0.98 - bank 0.125 = +0.855, against the required +0.10. The prose overstates how often v1 and v3 bring every piece into the first 2,000 characters (0.50 actual vs 0.775 and 0.699 stated) and how often the memory bank does at 24,000 characters (0.14 actual vs 0.32 stated).

unverified.title: '0.917 of training questions right, against 0.309 for v3' compares two different measures
unverified.evidence: Recomputed on mdtrain with measure(): v4's 0.917 is the per-question share (44/48 right), but v3's 0.309 is the pre-registered mean of the three group means. On one measure the figures are 0.927 vs 0.309 (group means) or 0.917 vs 0.188 (per question). The same sentence is repeated in FACTBANK_MULTI_RESULTS.md:97. The words results document notes the same mix-up for 0.688 vs 0.752, but not for this pair.
unverified.impact: No rule uses these numbers, so no decision changes. The stated v4-over-v3 gain on training is +0.608 where it should be +0.618 (group mean) or +0.729 (per question).

unverified.title: v4 walk-back rules are checked before the system filter, so a winning plan can answer with the start ticket's own field
unverified.evidence: candidates() checks 'every hop reaches something new' as `set(ents) <= came_from` on the unfiltered reach (line 238). execute() applies plan.system afterwards (lines 174-175), and that filter can leave only the start entity. inverse() (line 345) only recognises X / X_of pairs, so referenced_by -> linked_linear, which walks straight back, is not blocked. Example: mdblind issue_pr_author-author-017 has the winning plan ENG-4823 -> referenced_by -> linked_linear, which reaches [ENG-4823, ENG-4987]. The [linear] filter leaves only [ENG-4823], so the answer is ENG-4823's own assignee, 'Devon Price'; the expected PR author is 'Maya Chen'. The same thing happens in 033 (referenced_by reaches [ENG-9271, #437202], filtered to ENG-9271) and in 038. Counts of winning plans that, after the filter, answer only from what they started at or passed through: mdblind and mdblindchanged 5 per version (v4, v5 and v6 alike), including all 4 issue_pr_author questions and person_count-015. mdtrain has 3. mdfresh, mdwords and their changed copies have 0. The one right issue_pr_author answer on blind (021, 'Noah Patel') also comes from such a plan.
unverified.impact: No published number changes. I dropped these plans at answer time and kept the frozen weights: 2 answers change on each blind set, and all stay wrong. The means stay at v4 0.727, v5 0.769, v6 0.769 (changed copy 0.764, 0.769, 0.806). The blind issue_pr_author score (0.25) and pieces of the training fit, however, rest on plans that the pre-registered v4 rules ('may not answer with only what it started from') say are not allowed.

unverified.title: Planner.enrich caches by the question's word set alone, ignoring plain words, floor, type_floor and later combine/floor changes
unverified.evidence: The cache key is `frozenset(ws) | {'\0enrich'}`. Reproduction on the mdblind bank with the v6 lessons: on one planner, enrich(ws, ws, floor=0.9) and then enrich(ws, ws, floor=0.3) return the same object, which borrows nothing. A fresh planner at floor 0.3 borrows owner 0.44, author 0.41, next 0.39 and more. Calling enrich(ws, set()) also returns the cached object. Setting pl.combine='company' after the first call leaves the result the same. On the data, I found 0 questions in any of the 9 work folders whose word set equals another's while its plain words differ. dev_v6.py builds a new Planner for every (combine, floor) setting. The only call that passes floor= is in tests/test_factbank_multi.py line 181, on a fresh planner.
unverified.impact: Nothing published is affected. With the current code I re-ran every published plan answer (v3 to v6 on mdtrain, mdtest, mdchanged, mdfresh, mdfreshchanged, mdwords, mdwordschanged, mdblind and mdblindchanged), and all of them reproduce exactly. Re-learning plan_lessons_v6.json from mdtrain gives a file identical in every field. The defect is latent: a sweep that reuses one planner, or passes floor=, would silently report the first setting's results for every setting.

unverified.title: The 'no harm' rules are scored on the retest set, the same set used to develop and choose v5 and v6
unverified.evidence: Rule 5 of general_test (v6 >= v4 - 0.03 on the retest set) and rule 4 of words_test use mdfresh. That set was a development set for both methods: dev_v5.py for v5, and dev_v6.py, which chose among the allowed settings by a dev mean that includes it. The chosen setting (mean, 0.4) has the highest retest score of the 10 (0.657). The other nine score 0.631, 0.590 x3, 0.622, 0.622, 0.606, 0.622 and 0.622. In v5's development, a variant at 0.435 on the retest set was dropped; it would have failed rule 4 (threshold 0.596 - 0.03 = 0.566).
unverified.impact: No decision changes. All 10 v6 settings would pass rule 5 on the retest set (lowest 0.590, threshold 0.566), and the training half is 0.927 for every setting. By construction, though, the retest half of these rules cannot detect harm that development steered away from, so 'met' carries little evidence.

unverified.title: The single-document lessons used by v2 to v6 were trained on 4 documents of the first held-out multi-document test
unverified.evidence: Every plan arm loads TrainedBank(..., Lessons.load(fb50/lessons.json)). Its entity weights rank the content starts (trained.py lines 87-88; plans.candidates line 203). fb50 shares 4 dsids with mdtest (0abbd8a3..., 11fffe94..., 235cf21c..., e27f5622...) and 1 with mdtrain. Five fb50 training questions are about those documents (for example linear_due-005, linear_due-010 and linear_due-020). 10 of the 50 mdtest questions have one of them as a gold document. The multi-document pre-registration only says that mdtrain and mdtest share no document. fb50 overlaps none of mdfresh, mdwords or mdblind.
unverified.impact: No rule changes. The lessons hold 6 entity weights and associations from words to field names, with no values. On those 10 questions v3 scores 0 of 10 and v2 1 of 10. The first test's rules 1 and 2 were not met anyway. The retest, new-words and general-English results are unaffected.
